title: A review of advanced magnetic and conductive materials for enhancing PMSM performance
abstract: Abstract The Axial Flux Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motor (AF-PMSM) has emerged as a critical topology for electric traction due to its superior torque density; however, its performance limit is increasingly defined by material constraints rather than geometric design. This paper presents a comprehensive review and parametric sensitivity analysis of advanced core, magnet, and conductor materials to quantify their impact on motor efficiency and power density. A comparative investigation is conducted on a 2.5 kW single-stator single-rotor AF-PMSM, evaluating the electromagnetic trade-offs of Soft Magnetic Composites (SMC), Cobalt-Iron (CoFe) alloys, Nanocrystalline cores, and Carbon Nanotube (CNT) composite windings. The study reveals that the impact of core material is heavily coupled to the magnetic excitation source; while core selection yields negligible efficiency gains (< 1%) under low-flux ferrite excitation, the integration of high-energy NdFeB magnets amplifies material divergence, with CoFe cores enabling efficiencies up to 90.29% by mitigating saturation. The research reveals a synergistic performance peak: a configuration utilizing Vacoflux-50 cores, N52 magnets, and CNT-Copper composite windings attains a maximum efficiency of 93.61%. These findings demonstrate that the holistic integration of nanocomposites and advanced alloys is a prerequisite for achieving the aggressive power density targets of next-generation electric vehicles.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The automotive industry has increasingly standardized on Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motors (PMSMs) for EV powertrains, prioritizing their superior power-to-weight ratio and efficiency metrics of 92–97%. Unlike traditional induction motors, which rely on rotor windings to generate flux, PMSMs employ embedded permanent magnets. This configuration negates the rotor copper losses inherent in earlier technologies. Consequently, PMSMs offer the high-power density and robust performance required for rigorous traction applications, without the thermal and weight penalties associated with wound-rotor designs.

Despite the continuous evolution of propulsion technology, the fundamental topology of electrical machines has remained relatively stable. The true driver of innovation in high-power-density EV applications is now material selection, which dictates whether a design can meet strict volume and mass constraints. Consequently, developing PMSMs has evolved into a complex balancing act that weighs efficiency and thermal resilience against weight, manufacturability, and cost [ 1 ,  2 ]. The integration of advanced magnetic alloys and rare-earth permanent magnets has been pivotal in this regard, enabling sustained efficiencies above 95% that directly translate to extended driving ranges. However, these compact, high-output designs face severe thermal challenges; with operating temperatures frequently reaching 150–200 °C, effective heat dissipation is non-negotiable for maintaining stability. Simultaneously, the industry’s focus on mass reduction has spurred innovations in conductor materials and magnet compositions. These advancements allow modern PMSMs to typically achieve power densities between 0.3 and 0.5 kW/kg, while ongoing research into topology optimization seeks to push these boundaries even further [ 2 ,  3 ].

When benchmarked against alternative topologies—specifically Induction Motors (IMs), Switched Reluctance Motors (SRMs), and Synchronous Reluctance Motors (SynRMs)—PMSMs demonstrate superior torque and power density for a given volume [ 4 ]. This volumetric efficiency is a deciding factor for automotive engineers, as it enables sharper acceleration and more seamless integration into restricted chassis spaces. Yet, this performance comes at a premium. The architecture’s inherent reliance on rare-earth elements exposes manufacturers to supply chain volatility and sustainability critiques. In response, contemporary design philosophies are shifting toward mitigating these economic and environmental risks. The current focus has expanded to include the exploration of alternative magnet chemistries and recyclability protocols, aiming to decouple high-performance traction from an overdependence on critical raw materials.

The operational ceiling of a Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motor (PMSM) in electric vehicle (EV) powertrains specifically its efficiency limits, power density, and thermal boundaries is fundamentally governed by the materials selected for its active components: the electromagnetic core, copper windings, and permanent magnets [ 1 ]. As quantified in Fig.  1 , the intrinsic properties of these materials serve as the primary drivers of per-unit efficiency [ 5 ]. For example, integrating high-energy rare-earth magnets like NdFeB is a proven approach to minimizing rotor losses and establishing a high baseline efficiency [ 6 ]. Engineers can further enhance this baseline by substituting standard silicon steel with amorphous or nanocrystalline alloys. This specific material shift dramatically curtails the core loss component, which is the primary physical mechanism driving the 1.4% overall efficiency improvement at 1200 rpm [ 7 ].

Raw material potential, however, must be paired with precise geometric design. Factors such as rotor magnet placement, stator slot topology, and air-gap sizing dictate the underlying electromagnetic behavior. These parameters directly control the torque ripple and speed range required to sustain dynamic EV driving cycles [ 4 ,  8 ,  9 ]. Consequently, modern motor design is an intricate balancing act. Designers must select optimal combinations of advanced alloys (such as FeCoV) to meet aggressive performance targets, while simultaneously addressing urgent industry demands for lifecycle sustainability and reduced dependence on rare-earth elements [ 10 ]. This review outlines the material technologies that define the current performance envelope of Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motors (PMSMs) within the context of electric propulsion. The structural framework of this analysis rests on three pillars: core laminations, permanent magnets, and stator conductors. As conceptualized in Fig.  2 , the optimization of these domains is governed by specific intrinsic properties—namely permeability, coercivity, and conductivity—which serve as the direct precursors to system-level metrics like efficiency and torque density. The text evaluates the progression of stator core materials, moving from standard electrical steels to advanced Cobalt-Iron alloys and nanocrystalline structures, with a focus on minimizing hysteresis and parasitic eddy currents. Simultaneously, the discussion navigates the critical trade-offs between magnetic flux, thermal resilience, and supply chain security by contrasting high-energy rare-earth magnets (NdFeB, SmCo) against cost-stable alternatives like Ferrite and Alnico. Beyond magnetic components, the study critiques standard copper windings against emerging nanostructured composites, specifically Carbon Nanotube-Copper (CNT-Cu), to assess their capacity for mass reduction and superior conductivity. These theoretical perspectives are validated through a Finite Element Analysis (FEA) of a 2.5 kW Axial Flux PMSM; this case study demonstrates that the strategic substitution of active materials can yield an efficiency gain exceeding 20% alongside significant weight reduction, underscoring the necessity of integrated material selection in next-generation EV powertrain design.

To specifically quantify how intrinsic material properties drive motor-level performance metrics, such as efficiency, torque density, and thermal stability, this review moves beyond a general survey of materials. A systematic literature search was conducted utilizing three primary databases IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science—to aggregate high-impact research. While the search window was primarily set to 2015–2025 to capture recent material advancements, select seminal papers and standard testing protocols (e.g., older ASTM standards) were retained to establish accurate baselines. Search queries combined material classes with specific performance constraints, using keywords such as “PMSM core losses,” “soft magnetic composites (SMC),” “nanocrystalline stator,” “rare-earth-free permanent magnets,” and “carbon nanotube conductors”. To maintain scientific rigor, studies were filtered based on data availability; articles were required to provide verifiable quantitative data specifically electromagnetic characterization (B-H curves, loss coefficients), thermal conductivity, or experimental motor test results. Priority was given to studies comparing multiple material grades under identical test conditions, while papers focusing purely on control theory, inverter topologies, or theoretical designs lacking material-level analysis were excluded.

This article is structured to provide a granular analysis of these material domains and their collective impact on machine topology. Section  2  scrutinizes the evolution of Core Materials, evaluating the magnetic permeability and loss characteristics of traditional Silicon Steels against high-performance Cobalt-Iron alloys, Soft Magnetic Composites (SMC), and Nanocrystalline structures. Section  3  examines Permanent Magnet Materials, juxtaposing the high energy density of rare-earth grades (NdFeB, SmCo) with the supply-chain resilience of Ferrite and hybrid configurations. Section  4  investigates Conductor Materials, analyzing the conductivity-to-weight trade-offs of commercial copper and aluminum against emerging Carbon Nanotube (CNT) composites. Section  5  provides a Discussion and Synthesis, integrating these material properties into a holistic view of industrial trends, NVH (Noise, Vibration, and Harshness) considerations, and multi-objective optimization strategies. Section  6  presents a comprehensive Case Study, utilizing Finite Element Analysis (FEA) of a 2.5 kW Axial Flux PMSM to empirically validate the theoretical performance gains offered by advanced material substitution. Finally, Sect.  7  concludes the review with a summary of critical findings and an outlook on future research directions.

sections.heading: Core materials
paragraphs: In the context of high-speed PMSM operation, the selection of stator core material constitutes a critical design variable that governs both system efficiency and power density. Practically, this selection process is defined by a fundamental dichotomy between Iron Loss and Torque Density. As rotational frequencies increase, iron losses—specifically the cumulative effect of hysteresis and eddy currents—evolve into the primary thermal stressor. To mitigate these parasitic effects and maintain drive cycle efficiency, engineering strategies typically prioritize materials exhibiting high electrical resistivity or utilize ultra-thin lamination stacking. Conversely, torque density is intrinsic to the material’s Saturation Flux Density (B sat ). High- B sat  materials permit the design of narrower stator teeth without risking magnetic saturation, thereby maximizing the slot area available for copper windings and directly enhancing power output. To address these conflicting physical demands, the industry has developed a diverse spectrum of magnetic solutions. Figure  3  delineates the taxonomy of these core materials, encompassing traditional electrical steels, Cobalt-Iron (CoFe) and Nickel-Iron (NiFe) alloys, as well as advanced nanocrystalline structures, amorphous alloys, and Soft Magnetic Composites (SMC). Each category offers a distinct electromagnetic and thermal profile, establishing the comparative framework for the detailed performance analysis that follows.

A comparative analysis of the data in Table  2  reveals distinct performance boundaries for each material class. Cobalt-Iron (CoFe) variants, specifically VACOFLUX 27 and HIPERCO 50, establish the upper limit for magnetic saturation with flux densities reaching 2.38 T. This capability makes them indispensable for maximizing torque density, even though their electrical resistivity remains moderate (~ 0.15–0.40 µΩm). In stark contrast, Soft Magnetic Composites (SMCs) such as Somaloy 130i represent an extreme outlier in terms of loss mitigation; their unique insulated particle structure yields resistivity values up to 20,000 µΩm, effectively neutralizing eddy currents, albeit at a compromise of lower magnetic saturation (1.47 T). Bridging these extremes are the Amorphous and Nanocrystalline alloys (e.g., METGLAS and VITROPERM), which strike a strategic balance. These materials offer respectable flux densities (1.2–1.65 T) while maintaining resistivity levels (1.1–1.42 µΩm) that are approximately three times higher than standard electrical steels. Consequently, the data confirms that material selection is not a search for a universally superior alloy, but a targeted decision based on the specific frequency and thermal constraints of the application.

The magnetization behavior of these diverse core candidates is mapped in Fig.  4 , which correlates Magnetic Flux Density (B) against Field Strength (H) at a standardized ambient temperature of 20 °C. The empirical trajectories reveal a distinct hierarchy in magnetic capacity. Cobalt-Iron (CoFe) alloys—represented by the uppermost curves—unequivocally demonstrate the highest Saturation Flux Density (B sat ), peaking well above 2.0 Tesla. This superior saturation limit distinguishes CoFe as the premier choice for high-torque applications where maximizing magnetic flux within a confined volume is the primary objective. Building on this empirical overview, the following subsections dissect the specific electromagnetic behavior of each material class, systematically evaluating their viability against the rigorous performance and efficiency demands of modern electric vehicle traction.

sections.heading: Conventional electrical steels
paragraphs: Non-oriented (NO) silicon steels maintain their ubiquity as the foundational core material for traction motors, favored for their ability to balance magnetic efficiency with manufacturing scalability. Standard industrial grades, typically alloyed with 2–4 wt% silicon, deliver a robust saturation flux density of 1.7–1.9 T. Their core loss metrics—generally falling between 1.0 and 3.0 W/kg at 1.5 T (50 Hz)—are strictly governed by the silicon concentration and the intensity of the cold reduction process. The material’s electromagnetic profile is refined through a rigorous thermomechanical regimen that includes hot rolling, significant cold reduction (70–90%), decarburization, and batch annealing in the 750–800 °C range. This sequence is critical for controlling texture evolution; the goal is to orient grains to maximize permeability (reaching values up to 6500) while ensuring the random distribution necessary for isotropic motor performance. To further minimize hysteresis losses (< 0.8 W/kg), microstructural integrity is paramount. Manufacturers enforce strict purity protocols to keep precipitate-forming impurities—specifically aluminum nitride and niobium carbonitride—below 20 ppm, thereby reducing domain wall pinning. In advanced iterations, the formulation is modified with 0.1 wt% aluminum to boost electrical resistivity to 0.6 µΩ·m, a strategy that effectively curtails eddy-current losses by approximately 20% relative to conventional baselines [ 30 ,  31 ,  32 – 33 ].

sections.heading: Amorphous and nanocrystalline alloys
paragraphs: While silicon steels currently dominate the market, the push for higher operational frequencies has shifted attention toward amorphous and nanocrystalline alloys as the premier candidates for next-generation efficiency. Unlike their crystalline counterparts, amorphous ribbons—specifically the Fe₇₉Si₃B₁₄P₄, composition—are fabricated via rapid melt spinning. This process freezes the molten alloy into a completely disordered state, effectively eradicating magnetocrystalline anisotropy and domain-wall pinning. The result is a material with exceptional soft magnetic credentials: a saturation flux density (B sat ) of approximately 1.56 T, coercivity (H c ) below 2 A/m, and core losses suppressed to under 0.5 W/kg (at 1.0 T, 50 Hz).

The performance envelope is further expanded by nanocrystalline derivatives, such as the FINEMET alloy Fe₇₃.₅Cu₁Nb₃Si₁₅.₅B₇. Through a precise annealing window at 550–600 °C, this material develops 10–20 nm α-Fe(Si) grains suspended within an amorphous matrix. This dual-phase microstructure, stabilized by Copper-Niobium induced nucleation and Boron-Phosphorus glass formers, yields effective permeabilities (µ e ) exceeding 200,000 and maintains losses below 0.5 W/kg even at 100 kHz (B sat  ≈ 1.2–1.4 T). Further compositional tuning, such as the addition of 1 at% Cobalt, has been shown to boost flux density by 5% while lowering the optimal annealing temperature by 25 °C. At the frontier of this technology, additive manufacturing is being employed to create Fe–Si–B–P–Cu–Nb nanocomposites with graded microstructures. These advanced architectures achieve coercivities as low as 1 A/m with stability up to 200 kHz, positioning solutions like NANOMET cores as critical enablers for the high-frequency demands of future EV traction drives [ 34 ,  35 – 36 ].

sections.heading: Nikel-iron (NiFe) alloys
paragraphs: Nickel-Iron alloys, particularly the Permalloy class (Ni₈₀Fe₂₀) define the industry standard for high magnetic responsiveness. These materials are characterized by near-zero magnetostriction (< 3 × 10⁻⁶) and exceptional initial permeability (µ i  > 100,000) following a stress-relief annealing cycle at 300 °C, they typically achieve extremely low coercivity values (H c  < 8 A/m), indicating minimal hysteresis loss.

Recent advancements have focused on the galvanic synthesis of these alloys for specialized applications. Research into electrodeposited NiFe thin films, co-synthesized with platinum (Pt) complex additives in polyol baths, has yielded nanostructured grains in the 20–100 nm range. By carefully optimizing deposition current density and complexing agents, these films attain a maximum permeability (µₘₐₓ) exceeding 50,000, electrical resistivity (ρ) near 0.20 µΩ·m, and and coercivities below 40 A/m. Subsequent thermal processing is critical to their performance; post-deposition annealing at 250–350 °C alleviates internal lattice stresses, boosting saturation magnetization (Mₛ) to 800 emu/cm³ while further suppressing coercivity to approximately 16 A/m [ 37 ,  38 ,  39 – 40 ].

While their saturation flux densities are lower than silicon steels or CoFe alloys, the unique low-loss profile of NiFe alloys renders them indispensable for specific niches within the EV ecosystem. They are particularly suited for high-sensitivity magnetic sensors, electromagnetic shielding, and auxiliary low-frequency components where efficiency and Electromagnetic Compatibility (EMC) take precedence over raw torque generation.

sections.heading: Cobalt-iron (CoFe) alloys
paragraphs: For traction applications where maximizing power density is the non-negotiable priority, Cobalt-Iron alloys—commercialized as Hiperco50A or Vacoflux50—represent the industry benchmark. These equiatomic compositions (Co₄₉Fe₄₉V₂) are typically synthesized via vacuum arc melting and subsequent hot rolling to achieve a massive saturation flux density (B sat ) of 2.35 T. While maintaining a respectable electrical resistivity of approximately 0.40 µΩ·m, they manage to keep coercivity (H c ) below 10 A/m. The metallurgical strategy behind this performance relies on strategic doping with 2 at% Vanadium; this addition stabilizes the Body-Centered Cubic (BCC) phase and refines grain size to roughly 15 μm, effectively suppressing the brittle ordering transitions that historically plagued binary Co-Fe systems.

Modern fabrication techniques are further refining these properties. Research into Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) of CoFe-Phosphorous nanocrystalline alloys has yielded materials with B > 2.3 T and enhanced resistivity (ρ > 0.30 µΩ·m). The rapid thermal cycle inherent to SPS inhibits the precipitation of deleterious secondary phases like (CoFe)₂P which is critical for preserving soft magnetic behavior. Simultaneously, additive manufacturing via laser powder bed fusion is opening new frontiers with High-Entropy Alloys (CoFeAlMnCr) These multicomponent systems utilize entropy-stabilized solid solutions to achieve in-situ phase refinement, delivering flux densities near 1.8 T with coercivities below 87.5 A/m [ 41 ,  42 – 43 ]. The practical advantage of this chemistry is quantified in Fig.  5 , which maps core loss against flux density at 50 Hz. The data highlights a clear divergence at higher magnetic loads: while traditional silicon steels suffer from exponential loss increases as flux exceeds 1.0 T, Fe-Co alloys maintain stability. Notably, Vacoflux50 exhibits the lowest losses across the entire operational spectrum, empirically validating its status as the optimal material for high-flux, high-efficiency traction motors.

The efficiency gap between solid alloy laminations and composite structures is empirically mapped in Fig.  6 . Here, the core loss profiles of high-permeability Cobalt-Iron (Vacoflux 50) are benchmarked against four distinct grades of Somaloy Soft Magnetic Composites (SMCs) at a standard utility frequency of 50 Hz. The data reveals a significant divergence in performance under load. Vacoflux 50 exhibits remarkable linear stability, maintaining negligible losses that rise only marginally—from roughly 0.5 W/kg to just over 2 W/kg—even as flux density is pushed to its 2.0 T saturation limit. In contrast, the SMC variants face a steeper thermodynamic penalty due to their granular nature. While grades like Somaloy 1000 5P and 110 5P perform adequately at lower fields, their losses accelerate exponentially once flux density exceeds 1.0 T, culminating in values approaching 8–12 W/kg. This behavior highlights that, while SMCs offer unique geometric freedom, they incur a substantial efficiency cost compared to rolled CoFe alloys in low-frequency, high-flux regimes.

The functional trade-offs between solid alloys and composites are further elucidated by their magnetization behaviors, as plotted in Fig.  7 . This graph contrasts the magnetic flux density (B) against magnetic field intensity (H) for the Vacoflux 50 alloy versus the Somaloy composite series at ambient temperature. The disparity in magnetic susceptibility is stark. Vacoflux 50 exhibits a steep magnetization gradient, reaching its saturation plateau of ≈ 2.3 T with minimal field excitation; this indicates exceptional permeability and a sharp ‘saturation knee.’ Conversely, the Somaloy grades display a much more gradual, linear rise. To approach a comparable saturation level of 2.2 T, these composites require significantly elevated magnetic field intensities (H). This ‘sheared’ loop characteristic—typical of materials with distributed air gaps—signals reduced permeability and a slower rate of flux accumulation. Ultimately, this data reinforces a clear design bifurcation: Vacoflux 50 remains the superior candidate for high-flux density applications where maximizing torque per volume is critical, whereas Somaloy serves best in applications where the priority is complex 3D flux paths or geometric flexibility, even at the cost of saturation efficiency.

A holistic review of the data presented in Table  2  clarifies the distinct operational niches occupied by each material class. Cobalt-Iron alloys (e.g., Hiperco 50, Vacoflux) stand unrivaled at the performance apex, delivering flux densities exceeding 2.3 T. This capability makes them the default choice for ultra-compact, high-torque traction motors, albeit at a premium; their adoption requires a rigorous cost-benefit analysis to justify the significantly higher material and processing expenses. Conversely, Nickel-Iron alloys sacrifice flux capacity (~ 0.8–1.6 T) to prioritize magnetic responsiveness, offering the low coercivity and high permeability essential for specialized, low-loss subsystems. For high-frequency architectures, Amorphous and Nanocrystalline alloys emerge as the superior candidates, leveraging their elevated resistivity to drastically curtail core losses. Finally, Soft Magnetic Composites (SMCs) like the Somaloy series introduce a unique geometric advantage; their powder-based structure facilitates isotropic 3D flux paths, enabling complex topologies that traditional laminations cannot support. Ultimately, the comparative assessment underscores that no single material offers a panacea. Optimal selection is an exercise in equilibrium—balancing the competing demands of flux density, thermal stability, manufacturability, and cost against the specific duty cycle of the EV powertrain.

sections.heading: Soft magnetic composites (SMC)
paragraphs: Soft Magnetic Composites (SMCs) represent a fundamental departure from the laminated architecture of traditional cores. Fabricated from high-purity iron or alloy powders (typically 50–150 μm in diameter), these materials are encapsulated in a dielectric coating before being compacted and sintered into net-shape components. This granular structure grants engineers isotropic magnetic properties, enabling the design of complex 3D flux paths that are physically impossible to realize with planar steel sheets. The primary electromagnetic advantage of SMCs lies in their resistivity; the insulating layer separating each particle acts as a barrier to current flow, drastically suppressing eddy current losses and making the material exceptionally stable at high operational frequencies and rotational speeds. However, this segmentation comes at a cost: the non-magnetic insulation effectively creates a “distributed air gap” throughout the core volume, which results in a relative permeability significantly lower than that of continuous steel laminations [ 44 ,  45 – 46 ].

The performance of an SMC core is ultimately governed by the chemistry of its inter-particle coating. Manufacturers utilize both inorganic layers (such as magnesium oxide or phosphates) for thermal robustness and organic binders (like phenolic resins or epoxies) for mechanical integrity. The engineering challenge lies in optimizing this dielectric boundary: the coating must be thin enough to maintain high magnetic saturation but uniform enough to prevent electrical shorting between particles. Recent advancements in hybrid coatingsspecifically MgO-phenolic resin systems have successfully bridged this gap, offering substantial reductions in eddy current losses alongside improved thermal stability. Furthermore, the microstructure itself plays a defining role; smaller, uniformly coated particles have been shown to minimize hysteresis losses, particularly in high-frequency regimes. Despite the inherent compromise in permeability, the unique combination of geometric versatility, low high-frequency losses, and cost-effective manufacturing positions SMCs as a formidable competitor for the complex, high-speed magnetic topologies required by modern electric vehicle powertrains [ 44 ,  45 ,  47 ,  48 ].

sections.heading: Permanent magnet materials
paragraphs: The architecture of the rotor’s magnetic circuit serves as the governing variable for a traction motor, dictating both its peak torque capability and its thermal operational ceiling. Consequently, selecting a permanent magnet material is not a singular decision but a navigation of a complex optimization matrix that balances Electromagnetic Performance, Thermal Reliability, and Cost. The primary figure of merit, the Maximum Energy Product (BH) max  acts as a direct proxy for air-gap flux density; high-energy materials like Neodymium-Iron-Boron (NdFeB) are therefore prerequisites for achieving the compact, power-dense form factors required by modern EVs. However, under the stress of heavy loads or fault currents, the motor’s resistance to demagnetization is determined by the material’s Intrinsic Coercivity (H cj ) and its temperature coefficients. Given that rare-earth elements can constitute up to 50% of the active material cost, the industry is aggressively seeking to mitigate supply chain volatility—specifically by reducing dependence on heavy rare earths like Dysprosium and Terbium.

Beyond these magnetic metrics, the physical properties of the material—specifically thermal conductivity and mass density—exert a profound influence on system-level performance. Table  3  quantifies these parameters, highlighting distinct material behaviors. For instance, Alnico alloys function as excellent thermal conductors (46 W/m·K) capable of sustaining operations at 530–550 °C, a thermodynamic advantage that offsets their lower energy product. Conversely, Ferrite magnets offer a weight advantage with densities of just 4900 kg/m³; yet, their utility is constrained by significantly lower remanence (0.35–0.45 T) and poor thermal conductivity (~ 3.0 W/m·K). These trade-offs necessitate a holistic selection strategy that looks beyond simple magnetic strength to consider the overall power-to-weight ratio. sections.heading: Rare earth element- based magnets (NdFeB and SmCo)
paragraphs: In the hierarchy of commercial magnetic materials, Neodymium-Iron-Boron (NdFeB) occupies the apex, offering Maximum Energy Products (BH) max  that typically range from 398 to 437.8 kJ/m³. This extreme flux density is the primary enabler for the compact, high-torque architectures defining modern electric vehicle propulsion. However, this performance comes with a significant thermal vulnerability. NdFeB alloys exhibit acute temperature sensitivity; irreversible flux losses frequently onset beyond 120–150 °C as thermal activation overcomes the material’s inherent coercivity, creating a risk of catastrophic demagnetization under peak load conditions. The standard metallurgical countermeasure involves doping the alloy with Heavy Rare-Earth Elements (HREE) such as Dysprosium (Dy) or Terbium (Tb). This addition fortifies the magneto-crystalline anisotropy field, boosting coercivity beyond 1600 kA/m to ensure operational stability at elevated temperatures [ 49 ,  50 ,  51 ,  52 – 53 ]. Recent evaluations of switched-flux permanent magnet machines confirm that commercial N52 grades currently represent the optimal balance of remanence and coercive force, directly translating to superior machine efficiency [ 54 ].

Where NdFeB falters thermally, Samarium-Cobalt (SmCo) alloys provide the necessary resilience. The two primary variants, SmCo₅ and Sm₂Co₁₇, maintain operational integrity at temperatures reaching 250–300 °C and 350–550 °C, respectively. Their stability is quantified by remarkably low reversible temperature coefficients (approximately − 0.02 to − 0.03%/°C), which ensures consistent magnetic output despite the thermal cycling inherent to automotive traction. While intrinsic coercivity varies by processing method, optimized SmCo grades can surpass 1500 kA/m without the need for extensive doping. The trade-off lies in energy density: SmCo 5  typically delivers a (BH) max  between 127 and 199 kJ/m³, while the Sm₂Co₁₇ variant pushes this ceiling to 191–255 kJ/m³. Although these values fall short of NdFeB standards, the material’s immunity to corrosion and thermal degradation renders it indispensable for safety-critical, high-heat applications [ 55 ,  56 ]. Together, these two rare-earth families form the bedrock of high-performance PMSM design [ 57 ].

The industry consensus currently positions NdFeB as the dominant generalist due to its superior cost-to-strength ratio, while SmCo is reserved for specialized environments where thermal reliability is non-negotiable. Beyond chemistry, ongoing research into nanostructuring seeks to further enhance these magnets by minimizing the microstructural defects that serve as nucleation sites for demagnetization [ 58 ]. However, the dominance of rare-earth technologies is shadowed by a complex supply chain. The extraction and refining processes are energetically intensive and generate significant hazardous waste, contributing to a heavy ecological footprint [ 59 ]. Furthermore, the geopolitical concentration of these resources primarily within China creates a strategic bottleneck for global automotive manufacturers [ 60 ]. In response, the industry is accelerating the development of circular economy solutions. While full-scale recycling remains technologically immature, pilot initiatives like VALOMAG (Valorization of Magnets) are establishing integrated recovery systems to reclaim high-value alloys from end-of-life vehicles [ 61 ,  62 – 63 ]. Parallel to these recovery efforts, advanced diagnostic techniques are being deployed to monitor in-service degradation, aiming to extend the functional lifespan of the magnets currently in use [ 64 ].

sections.heading: Alternative magnet materials (ferrite and novel geometries)
paragraphs: As the industry seeks to decouple from rare-earth dependency, legacy materials are being re-evaluated through the lens of modern engineering. Aluminum-Nickel-Cobalt (Alnico) alloys have historically served as the benchmark for thermal resilience. Their ability to maintain stability in high-heat environments makes them theoretically attractive; however, their intrinsic magnetic limitations prevent widespread adoption in traction scenarios. With a coercivity generally below 160 kA/m and a moderate Maximum Energy Product (BH) max  of roughly 80 kJ/m³, Alnico struggles to resist the strong demagnetizing fields inherent to high-power density motors. While advanced processing techniques such as additive manufacturing and controlled solid-state alignment—are currently being explored to boost these metrics, Alnico remains competitively disadvantaged against rare-earth baselines in terms of pure power density [ 65 ,  66 ,  67 – 68 ].

In contrast, Ferrite (ceramic) magnets offer a value proposition defined by economic abundance and chemical inertia. These materials boast superior corrosion resistance and widely accessible raw materials, alongside respectable thermal stability up to 300 °C. The thermodynamic penalty, however, is severe: with a remanent flux density typically below 0.4 T and a (BH) max  rarely exceeding 32 kJ/m³, standard surface-mounted ferrite designs cannot meet the torque-per-volume requirements of a performance EV [ 75 ].

To bridge this performance gap, engineers are turning to geometric compensation. Since the material itself lacks density, the solution lies in flux-concentrating rotor topologies. Architectures such as the “spoke-type” rotor allow for a greater volume of magnet material to be embedded within the core, effectively focusing the magnetic flux to rival the output of rare-earth counterparts [ 76 ]. Research confirms that when paired with these optimized configurations, Ferrite-based PMSMs can successfully fulfill both traction and auxiliary demands with competitive efficiency [ 77 ,  78 – 79 ]. Furthermore, specific design refinements—such as sophisticated yoke structuring and core skewing—have proven effective in neutralizing parasitic effects like cogging torque [ 78 ]. Consequently, Ferrite technology remains a viable, strategic option for cost-sensitive segments where supply chain sovereignty is the overriding priority [ 80 ,  81 ].

sections.heading: Advanced  magnet technologies (bonded, composite, hybrid ma gnets)
paragraphs: Driven by the imperative to mitigate rare-earth supply risks and dampen cost volatility, the industry is increasingly pivoting toward hybrid and advanced magnet architectures. Bonded magnets represent a fundamental shift in fabrication; by suspending magnetic powders (NdFeB or Ferrite) within a polymer matrix, manufacturers can utilize injection molding to achieve complex, net-shape geometries that are impossible with brittle sintered ceramics. This capability unlocks significant geometric freedom for custom, compact motor designs [ 82 ]. However, this mechanical flexibility incurs a thermodynamic penalty: the polymer binder inherently limits the thermal stability and maximum operating temperature of the assembly compared to fully dense metallic magnets [ 83 ].

To bridge the performance gap between low-flux ferrite and high-cost rare earths, Composite Magnets are emerging as a balanced alternative. These materials employ a synergistic blending strategy, introducing small fractions of Rare Earth Elements (REEs) into a ferrite base to boost magnetic output while maintaining resource efficiency [ 84 ]. Furthermore, Hybrid Bonded variants improve mechanical resilience and corrosion resistance—critical factors for extending service life in harsh automotive environments [ 85 ]. By carefully tuning the ratio of constituents, engineers can optimize the remanence-to-coercivity profile for specific duty cycles [ 86 ]. Beyond material blending, Hybrid Topologies are being implemented at the system level; these designs spatially integrate high-coercivity magnets (to resist demagnetization) with high-flux magnets (to generate torque) within the same rotor, reducing total rare-earth consumption without compromising reliability. These complex architectures are increasingly enabled by Additive Manufacturing, which permits the fabrication of high-density, near-net-shape components with minimal material waste [ 87 ].

A holistic review of Table  3  reveals the distinct operational niches defined by these material classes. NdFeB magnets (both conventional and advanced) remain the undisputed leaders in Maximum Energy Product (BH) max , making them the prerequisite for high-torque-density EV powertrains; however, their thermal fragility remains a limiting factor compared to Samarium-Cobalt (SmCo). While SmCo offers lower peak energy, its exceptional stability at elevated temperatures renders it indispensable for extreme traction conditions where cooling is constrained. Conversely, Ferrite and Alnico occupy the utility end of the spectrum, offering economic and environmental resilience at the cost of magnetic strength. To address the inherent weaknesses of NdFeB, the industry is deploying advanced metallurgical techniques—such as Grain Boundary Diffusion and doping with Dysprosium (Dy) or Terbium (Tb). These interventions significantly enhance coercivity and thermal endurance, effectively shifting the performance curve. Ultimately, the data confirms that material selection is not a binary choice but a complex optimization weighing cost, thermal ceilings, and the specific torque density required by the vehicle platform.

sections.heading: Conductor materials
paragraphs: While the magnetic circuit’s performance is bound by the core and magnet properties, it is the stator conductor that establishes the definitive efficiency ceiling for the electric circuit. In high-torque traction motors, Joule heating (I 2 R losses) typically constitutes the dominant loss mechanism; consequently, material selection is a dual optimization of minimizing DC resistance and maximizing thermal throughput. The industry benchmark remains the International Annealed Copper Standard (IACS) conductivity of 58 MS/m. Surpassing this threshold is critical, as any reduction in resistance directly translates to higher continuous ampacity without a corresponding thermal penalty. Simultaneously, modern EV powertrains are pushing slot current densities beyond 25 A/mm 2 . At these intensities, the conductor acts as a primary heat pipe; therefore, high thermal conductivity is non-negotiable for transferring thermal energy from the active slot region to the cooling jacket and preventing insulation failure.

To navigate these requirements, Fig.  9  taxonomizes the material landscape into two primary domains: established metallic conductors and emerging Carbon Nanotube (CNT) composites. Traditional options—Copper, Aluminum, Silver, and Gold—are defined by the trade-off between conductivity and scarcity. While Silver (63 MS/m) and Gold represent the theoretical apex of metallic conduction, their prohibitive cost restricts them to specialist contacts, leaving Copper as the commercial standard due to its optimal balance of performance and manufacturability. The frontier of research, however, lies in advanced composites. Hybrid architectures like Copper-CNT (CNT-Cu) and Aluminum-CNT (CNT-Al) are being developed to break the intrinsic limits of pure metals, offering superior electrical and thermal transport properties while maintaining structural integrity at elevated temperatures. This classification framework underpins the subsequent assessment of how each material class addresses the critical trade-offs between electrical efficiency, mass reduction, and economic feasibility in next-generation PMSM systems.

sections.heading: Electrical conductivity and related losses
paragraphs: Copper remains the ubiquitous standard for traction motor windings, leveraged for its exceptional conductivity (~ 59–60 MS/m). This material property is the primary defense against resistive (I 2 R) losses; however, even with copper’s efficiency, resistive heating remains the dominant thermodynamic bottleneck, often accounting for 70–75% of total machine losses under high-current loads [ 88 ,  89 ].

While copper defines the efficiency baseline, Aluminum offers a compelling alternative for mass-critical applications. With a density of just ~ 2.7 g/cm³ (vs. copper’s 8.9 g/cm³), aluminum windings can achieve substantial system weight reduction. The compromise lies in conductivity (~ 37 MS/m, roughly 60% of copper), which inherently increases resistive losses for a given wire gauge. To mitigate this, engineers employ a geometric compensation strategy: utilizing larger conductor cross-sections or compacted wire profiles to maximize the slot fill factor. This approach restores a portion of the electrical efficiency while preserving the significant gravimetric advantage [ 90 ].

Precious metals like Silver (~ 62.1 MS/m) and Gold (~ 45 MS/m) represent the theoretical ceiling of conductivity, but their prohibitive cost and scarcity relegate them to the status of reference standards rather than practical winding materials. Instead, material innovation is currently focused on Additive Manufacturing (AM) compatible alloys. Copper-based CuCr1Zr (precipitation-hardened with Cr and Zr) and Aluminum-based AlSi10Mg are gaining traction. While they exhibit slightly lower conductivity than their pure parent metals, they possess superior mechanical strength and processability. Their primary advantage is geometric; these alloys enable the printing of windings with integrated internal cooling channels, a thermal management feat impossible with conventional wire drawing [ 91 ]. The frontier of conductivity lies in Carbon Nanotube-Copper (CNT-Cu) composites. By integrating CNTs into a copper matrix—typically via solution mixing or ball milling to ensure uniform dispersion—researchers have created conductors that exceed the electrical and thermal limits of pure copper. This hybrid microstructure not only lowers resistive losses but also significantly augments mechanical strength, ensuring winding integrity under the high thermal and centrifugal stresses of next-generation electric machines.

sections.heading: Fabrication of carbon nanotube composites
paragraphs: The limitations of monolithic metals have driven the development of nanostructured composites that decouple mass from performance. When evaluating these advanced conductors for motor applications, their final operational properties rather than their fabrication methodologies dictate their utility. For stator windings, Carbon Nanotube-Copper (CNT-Cu) composites present a major leap in electrical and structural capability. The resulting material achieves a density of just ~ 5.2 g/cm³ (vs. 8.9 g/cm³ for pure Cu) while maintaining an electrical conductivity of 4.7 × 10⁵ S/cm. Most critically, the CNT network effectively cages the copper grain boundaries, mitigating electromigration and boosting ampacity to 6 × 10⁸ A/cm² nearly 100 times that of pure copper [ 92 ,  93 – 94 ].Parallel efforts in aluminum matrices focus on enhancing mechanical and thermal resilience. The optimized CNT-Al composite (with ~ 2 wt% CNT loading) delivers a tensile strength of 300 MPa and an electrical conductivity of 20–25 MS/m. By establishing efficient load-transfer networks, these composites offer a lightweight, high-strength alternative for PMSM windings where centrifugal forces are a concern [ 95 ,  96 – 97 ].

Beyond nanotubes, research is expanding into graphene-reinforced systems. Aluminum-Graphene composites have demonstrated thermal conductivity enhancements exceeding 125% with as little as 1 wt% graphene addition, attributing this boost to the formation of continuous conductive networks that bridge grain boundaries [ 107 ,  108 – 109 ]. Both composite varieties sustain or enhance conductivity compared to pure aluminium by reducing interface resistance and optimizing filler distribution, which also aids in improving thermal stability at high temperatures [ 95 ,  96 – 97 ]. Similarly, pure Graphene thin films [ 102 ,  103 ] carbon fibre-graphene reinforced polymers [ 104 ] and CNT-reinforced silicon rubber nanocomposites [ 110 ] are being evaluated as next-generation thermal interface materials, promising to resolve the heat extraction bottlenecks in high-power density motors. sections.heading: Thermal conductivity and heat dissipation
paragraphs: Effective thermal management is the linchpin of motor reliability, as the resistive losses inherent to the windings generate substantial heat loads that directly threaten the longevity of the insulation system. Copper serves as the primary defense in this thermodynamic battle; its high thermal conductivity (~ 390 W/m·K) acts as a natural heat sink, efficiently wicking thermal energy away from the active slot region to maintain winding temperatures below the critical 150 °C threshold [ 93 ,  111 ]. In contrast, Aluminum presents a thermal challenge with a conductivity of only ~ 237 W/m·K. However, this deficiency can be engineered around; in advanced axial flux topologies, aluminum windings are often paired with integrated cooling channels, utilizing active fluid dynamics to compensate for the material’s lower intrinsic diffusivity [ 91 ,  112 ].

The frontier of thermal engineering, however, lies in composite matrices. Research into graphene and carbon fiber-reinforced polymers indicates that these materials can provide a “thermal bridge” within the winding assembly. Specifically, carbon fiber-graphene hybrids have demonstrated a 28% increase in thermal conductivity coupled with surface electrical conductivities near 175 S/m, significantly enhancing in-plane heat transfer [ 104 ]. Furthermore, the insulation itself is evolving; epoxy resins doped with Hexagonal Boron Nitride (HBN) fillers are now being utilized to handle simultaneous thermal and electrical loads. HBN is unique in that it boosts thermal conductivity without compromising dielectric strength, preserving the insulation’s integrity under high-voltage stress [ 113 ]. Comprehending these thermal-mechanical interactions is a prerequisite for ensuring durability; however, thermal stability is only half the equation.

sections.heading: Mechanical strength and durability
paragraphs: In the high-dynamic environment of an EV traction motor, the conductor must withstand significant mechanical stressors, primarily driven by Lorentz forces during torque spikes and centrifugal loads at high rotational speeds. Pure Copper sets the baseline with a tensile strength of 210–250 MPa; however, pure Aluminum’s inherent softness (70–120 MPa) severely restricts its viability in high-vibration or high-speed rotor applications [ 99 ]. To expand the operational envelope, materials engineering has bifurcated into two reinforcement strategies: 1). Alloying: Precipitation-hardened conductors, such as CuCr1Zr and AlSi10Mg, offer a pragmatic compromise, boosting mechanical yield strength while maintaining acceptable conductivity levels [ 91 ]. Similarly, Aluminum-Iron alloys (e.g., Al–1.7 wt% Fe) have emerged as a solution for lightweighting applications that require greater structural rigidity than pure aluminum can provide. 2). Nanocomposites: The most dramatic gains are realized through nanocomposites. Carbon Nanotube (CNT) reinforced copper can achieve tensile strengths approximating 450 MPa—roughly 1.6 times that of the pure metal—without significant conductivity penalties.

At the polymer frontier, graphene foam-reinforced epoxies and lyotropic liquid crystalline polymer-CNT fibers are offering unprecedented electro-mechanical stability for specialized stator insulations [ 114 ,  115 ]. It is important to note that for Additive Manufacturing (AM) variants, mechanical performance is often contingent on post-processing; rigorous surface treatments are essential to eliminate porosity, restore conductivity, and ensure the dielectric integrity of the insulation layer [ 116 ,  117 ]. With these mechanical hurdles addressed, the pathway is now open for the commercial integration of these advanced conductors.

sections.heading: Discussion and synthesis
paragraphs: The comparative analysis conducted in this study establishes a deterministic link between intrinsic material physics and macroscopic machine performance. The selection of core, magnet, and winding materials does not merely alter static parameters; it fundamentally defines the dynamic capabilities of the Axial Flux Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motor (AF-PMSM). In high-speed operational domains, efficiency is predominantly governed by iron losses. The strategic transition from traditional Silicon Steel to Cobalt-Iron alloys or Soft Magnetic Composites (SMC) represents a significant mechanism for reducing hysteresis and eddy current losses, thereby extending the motor’s high-efficiency map. The achievable torque density is linearly proportional to the air-gap flux density (B g ). This parameter serves as the functional ceiling of the magnetic circuit, determined jointly by the remanence of the permanent magnet (the source) and the saturation limit of the core material (the capacity). Beyond electromagnetics, the physical attributes of the materials dictate the mechanical signature of the machine. Specific power is intrinsically linked to material mass density, while the Noise, Vibration, and Harshness (NVH) profile is a direct derivative of the core material’s magnetostriction coefficient. While current material combinations offer substantial performance, the optimization landscape remains constrained by inherent physical trade-offs. Addressing these remaining limitations requires a dual-focus approach: targeted future research into fundamental material science and a critical analysis of emerging industrial trends.

sections.heading: Dimensional optimization for high torque density
paragraphs: To maximize torque density without increasing the outer diameter, the design must maximize the air-gap flux density B g . However, increasing magnet thickness of 8 mm to boost B g  increases material cost C mat  and rotor mass M tot . The optimization identifies that increasing the stator slot fill factor via hairpin windings from 0.45 to 0.7 effectively increases the electric loading A electrical  without altering the core dimensions, providing the most cost-effective path to higher torque density within the fixed volume constraints.

sections.heading: Noise, vibration, and harshness (NVH) considerations
paragraphs: The acoustic signature of an AF-PMSM is not a singular metric but the output of a complex multi-physics interaction involving electromagnetic excitation, structural dynamics, and material response.

Consequently, the design imperative to maximize torque density—by utilizing high-remanence NdFeB magnets and high-saturation Cobalt-Iron cores—creates an inherent NVH penalty. Higher magnetic loading exponentially amplifies the attractive forces between rotor and stator, leading to increased radial deformation of the stator yoke. Simultaneously, Electric Loading introduces a secondary excitation source via the inverter. Time-harmonic currents, injected by the Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) switching strategy, interact with the spatial harmonics of the magnetic flux. This interaction generates torque ripple—a periodic oscillation that manifests as low-frequency vibration. While increasing electric loading boosts power density, it inescapably amplifies these harmonic forces.

The amplitude of the resulting vibration is dictated by how the core material physically responds to the magnetic field. While Cobalt-Iron alloys provide superior saturation, they exhibit a significantly higher magnetostriction coefficient (λ) compared to silicon steels. This leads to larger physical expansions and contractions of the crystal lattice during magnetization cycles, creating a source of “hum” independent of air-gap forces. Soft Magnetic Composites offer a distinct benefit in this domain. Their isotropic nature suppresses the eddy currents induced by high-frequency switching harmonics. Furthermore, the microstructural composition—iron particles insulated by a polymer matrix—provides enhanced internal mechanical damping. Unlike solid metal laminations, this structure acts as a passive damper, effectively dissipating vibrational energy and attenuating high-frequency acoustic transmission.

sections.heading: Future work
paragraphs: To bridge the gap between theoretical potential and industrial deployment, future research must address specific trade-offs across the magnetic, electric, and thermal domains. The limitations of 2D laminar flux are driving a shift toward isotropic powder metallurgy. Research is prioritizing the refinement of Soft Magnetic Composites (SMC), specifically Somaloy and Sumitomo Electric’s HB series; optimizing particle size distribution and insulating coatings is critical to mitigating eddy current losses and enabling the intricate 3D stator geometries required for high-speed traction [ 117 ,  119 ,  120 ]. Simultaneously, material science is converging with structural design through spatially optimized stators. By integrating hybrid materials—such as nanocrystalline yokes (Metglas, Finemet) with silicon steel teeth—engineers aim to localize magnetic properties where they are most needed. This effort is supported by the development of gradient magnetic materials and anisotropic microstructures, which facilitate precise flux control and defect minimization [ 54 ,  121 ,  122 ,  123 ,  124 ,  125 ,  126 – 127 ]. To accelerate these discoveries, Machine Learning (ML) algorithms are being deployed alongside Finite Element Analysis (FEA) to predict optimal compositions with superior flux control [ 128 ,  129 ,  130 – 131 ]. At the system level, these innovations are coalescing into dual three-phase topologies, where optimized pole-slot arrangements and integrated fault detection aim to push power density efficiency toward 94% under natural cooling [ 132 ,  133 ,  134 – 135 ].

The sustainability mandate necessitates a decoupling of performance from heavy rare-earth content. Research must persist in refining Dysprosium-free (Dy-free) NdFeB alloys via hot deformation and Grain Boundary Diffusion (GBD) using Terbium, which has demonstrated coercivity gains of ~ 49% [ 53 ,  136 ,  137 ]. Parallel efforts should focus on surface engineering—specifically the precise regulation of oxidation layers to create multi-layered grain boundary structures that enhance corrosion resistance without compromising magnetic output [ 138 ]. Manufacturing innovation is also key; correlating Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF) parameters (e.g., overlap ratio) with microstructural density will unlock complex, net-shape magnet geometries. Furthermore, the application of multi-head attention regression algorithms to forecast properties like remanence and coercivity based on impurity profiles will be instrumental in expediting the design of high-performance, resource-efficient grades [ 139 ].

For conductors, the challenge shifts from discovery to industrial scalability. Future work must concentrate on creating economical, reproducible synthesis methods that ensure the uniform dispersion and stable bonding of CNT and graphene fillers within metal matrices. Validating the reliability of these composites is paramount; comprehensive experimental studies are required to quantify degradation mechanisms under the rigorous heat cycling and mechanical vibration of aerospace and automotive duty cycles. Finally, the design loop must be closed with enhanced multiphysics modeling. Integrating heat transfer dynamics with insulation degradation behaviors will facilitate predictive maintenance strategies, while investigating conductor segmentation and novel winding topologies remains crucial for minimizing high-frequency AC losses in compact, power-dense machines [ 140 ,  141 ,  142 ,  143 – 144 ].

sections.heading: Industrial trends
paragraphs: While While nanocomposites represent the theoretical horizon, the immediate trajectory of industrial EV motor design is defined by the optimization of established materials. Copper remains the incumbent standard for traction windings due to its superior conductivity and established supply chain. However, the application of copper has shifted radically. Leading manufacturers, including Tesla (Model 3/Y), have transitioned from conventional round-wire windings to hairpin technology. By utilizing rectangular conductors, engineers can increase the slot fill factor from a traditional 0.45–0.50 to approximately 0.70. This geometric efficiency yields a ~ 20% improvement in space utilization and a 1–2% gain in overall motor efficiency [ 145 ,  146 – 147 ].

This topology is now ubiquitous across the premium sector; the BMW i3 (181 hp), Nissan Leaf (147 hp), and Jaguar I-PACE all leverage copper winding architectures to maximize torque density within constrained thermal envelopes [ 146 ]. Simultaneously, a parallel design philosophy is emerging for cost-sensitive and mass-market platforms: the pivot to Aluminum. While aluminum suffers from lower conductivity (~ 60% IACS), its gravimetric advantages are being unlocked through advanced shaping. Automotive manufacturers are adopting Aluminum Hairpins, where the maximized fill factor (0.70) partially offsets the resistive penalty of the material [ 148 ]. Furthermore, research by the Fraunhofer Institute highlights the potential of Cast Aluminum Coils; utilizing flat conductor configurations, these coils improve the thermal coupling between the winding and the laminated core, realizing a 30% boost in torque and a 20% enhancement in continuous power despite the higher electrical resistance of the base metal [ 149 ].

Conductor evolution does not occur in a vacuum; it is co-evolving with core and rotor technologies. The shift toward Soft Magnetic Composites (SMC) is complementing advanced windings. Unlike steel laminations restricted to 2D flux flow, isotropic SMCs enable modular stator architectures with 3D flux paths, effectively minimizing the volume of inactive copper in the end-windings [ 150 ]. To mitigate supply chain volatility, the industry is validating Dysprosium-free NdFeB grades (UH/EH series) that utilize Grain Boundary Diffusion to maintain coercivity > 180 °C. Additionally, Bonded Magnet Rotors are gaining traction in high-speed applications; their polymer-bonded structure inherently suppresses eddy current losses, offering a strategic alternative to sintered magnets [ 151 ].

Looking toward the 2025 targets set by the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE)—which mandate an eightfold increase in electric drive power density—research is pivoting to Copper-Carbon Nanotube (Cu-CNT) composites. Prototypes developed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory exhibit a 14% increase in ampacity over pure copper, offering a pathway to drastically reduce motor volume while meeting next-generation power requirements.

The comparative analysis presented in Table  4  consolidates the trade-offs between conductivity, thermal management, and mechanical strength across these material classes. The data suggests that while classic metals (Copper, Aluminum) will continue to dominate the commercial sector through geometric innovation (hairpins), the integration of nanocomposites and advanced manufacturing (AM) is poised to redefine the efficiency limits of the Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motor. Ultimately, the future of EV propulsion lies not in a single “super-material,” but in the holistic optimization of the magnetic, electrical, and thermal domains.

Beyond material substitution, the industrial landscape is witnessing a structural paradigm shift toward topological optimization to overcome the inherent weight penalties of iron cores. The commercial maturation of the Yokeless and Segmented Armature (YASA) axial flux topology represents a definitive pivot in the high-performance sector. By eliminating the inactive iron mass of the stator yoke and utilizing modular pole segments, this architecture delivers specific torque densities significantly exceeding conventional radial flux counterparts—a potential validated by Mercedes-Benz’s strategic acquisition of YASA Limited for its upcoming AMG electric portfolio. Parallel to this, the Printed Circuit Board (PCB) Stator is emerging as a viable alternative for weight-critical and auxiliary applications. Pioneered by innovators like Infinitum and ECM, this air-core technology replaces traditional copper windings and heavy iron laminations with etched conductive pathways on multi-layer circuit boards. This approach not only effectively eliminates cogging torque and iron losses but also allows for fully automated, “printed” manufacturing processes, offering a scalable pathway for ultra-lightweight traction systems that decouple performance from heavy metal supply chains.

A significant development in modern electric machine design is the integration of Printed Circuit Board (PCB) stators within Axial Flux Permanent Magnet (AFPM) architectures. By substituting the conventional iron core and wound copper coils with etched conductive layers on an FR-4 substrate, this topology eliminates the ferromagnetic stator teeth entirely. Consequently, commercial implementations of this “air-core” design have demonstrated the potential to reduce active motor mass by approximately 50% to 70% relative to equivalent radial flux machines [ 152 ].

From a loss-analysis perspective, the removal of the iron core inherently suppresses stator hysteresis and eddy current losses, allowing these systems to achieve IE5 Ultra-Premium efficiency levels. Reports indicate that this performance is attainable with a 66% to 80% reduction in copper usage, mitigating raw material costs [ 152 ,  153 ]. Additionally, the absence of magnetic interaction between the rotor magnets and steel teeth results in zero cogging torque, a critical characteristic for applications requiring high-precision motion control and minimal acoustic noise [ 154 ].

sections.heading: Inferences
paragraphs: The synthesis of contemporary material technologies leads to a definitive conclusion: elevating PMSM performance is no longer a function of isolated component optimization, but of holistic system integration. The interaction between electromagnetic physics, thermal ceilings, and manufacturing constraints has become the governing dynamic of modern motor design.

A systematic evaluation of the material landscape reveals a clear dichotomy. On one hand, advanced candidates like Cobalt-Iron (CoFe) alloys and Carbon Nanotube (CNT) composites occupy the theoretical apex, offering the highest potential for specific power and efficiency. However, their widespread adoption remains throttled by prohibitive costs and processing complexities. On the other hand, the industry is pivoting toward pragmatic hybrid architectures—specifically Soft Magnetic Composites (SMC) and rare-earth-reduced magnets—which offer a scalable equilibrium between performance and sustainability.

Ultimately, the trajectory of electric propulsion will not be defined solely by the discovery of new materials, but by the maturation of processing techniques. The primary challenge for the next decade is to bridge the “lab-to-fab” gap, translating the exceptional properties of nanocomposites and advanced alloys into reproducible, industrial-scale production realities.

sections.heading: Loss analysis of baseline motor
paragraphs: The static and dynamic electromagnetic behaviors of the baseline motor are visualized in Fig.  10 . Figure  10 (a) presents the 3D topology of the Single-Stator Single-Rotor (SSSR) assembly, while Fig.  10 (b) maps the corresponding magnetic flux density distribution. The simulation reveals a peak field intensity of approximately 2.304 T, with the highest flux concentrations localized at the stator tooth tips and magnet edges. This intensity gradient confirms robust magnetic coupling and effective flux linkage across the active air-gap region. Conversely, the cooler (lower density) zones demarcate the leakage paths where the magnetic circuit is less active. Notably, the concentration of flux around the pole tips points to incipient magnetic saturation; while currently minor, this suggests that future design iterations could further refine the stator geometry or magnet shaping to flatten these peaks and achieve a more uniform thermal and magnetic load.

The finite element mesh was generated subsequent to material assignment and geometric definition, as depicted in Fig.  11 . The temporal performance of the windings is captured in Fig.  12 , which illustrates the transient stator currents for phases A, B, and C. The waveforms exhibit a stable, balanced three-phase sinusoidal profile, validating the integrity of the winding distribution. However, minor harmonic distortions are observable in the wave shape. These artifacts are intrinsic to the interaction between the discrete permanent magnets and the variable inductance of the stator slots, confirming the presence of expected slotting effects during continuous dynamic operation.

The dynamic temporal stability of the machine’s magnetic parameters is analyzed in Fig.  13 , which plots the evolution of the direct-axis (L d ) and quadrature-axis (L q ) inductances over a 12 ms window. Both parameters exhibit a transient settling period before establishing a quasi-steady-state oscillation. Notably, the L q  component (green trace) maintains a marginally higher amplitude than L d  (red trace), confirming the presence of magnetic saliency in the rotor architecture. The pronounced, periodic ripples observed in the steady state are predominantly driven by slotting effects and local magnetic saturation; as the rotor magnets traverse the stator teeth, the effective reluctance of the magnetic circuit varies cyclically. Quantifying these dynamic fluctuations is a prerequisite for high-performance Field Oriented Control (FOC), as errors in inductance estimation can lead to detuning in the current control loops and inaccuracies in torque production.

The mechanical culmination of these electromagnetic forces is presented in Fig.  16 , which maps the motor’s torque production over the simulation window. The transient response exhibits a characteristic startup profile: an initial impulse peak followed by settling oscillations as the system stabilizes into its steady-state trajectory. Under the nominal operating conditions (3900 rpm) and utilizing the standard material set (M19 Steel, Ceramic 8D, Copper-75 C), the simulation confirms the following baseline metrics: Output Power: ≈ 2.5 kW, Rated Torque: 6.12 Nm (peaking at 6.12168 Nm), Maximum Efficiency: 67.58%. These values serve as the Control Benchmark. With the validity of the electromagnetic model established, the study proceeds to a parametric sensitivity analysis. To rigorously evaluate how material selection alters this performance envelope, three distinct investigative sweeps were conducted: Assessing the impact of permeability and losses (e.g., Cobalt-Iron vs. Silicon Steel), Evaluating flux density vs. cost trade-offs (e.g., NdFeB vs. Ferrite) and Analyzing the efficiency/mass balance (e.g., CNT composites vs. Copper).

sections.heading: Influence of core materials in AF-PMSM
paragraphs: The first phase of the sensitivity analysis focuses on the magnetic circuit’s reluctance and loss characteristics. To ensure a comprehensive evaluation, a representative high-performance grade was selected from each principal category of soft magnetic materials. The selection criteria prioritized materials capable of delivering high magnetic saturation (B sat ) while minimizing coercive force (H c ). The specific test candidates are Silicon Steel (SiFe): 10JNHF600, Nickel-Iron (NiFe): Permalloy 2mil, Cobalt-Iron (CoFe): Vacoflux50 (0.35 mm), Amorphous Alloy: Metglas 2605HB1M, Nanocrystalline: Finemet FT-3 M and Soft Magnetic Composite (SMC): Somaloy 700 h (5P @ 800 MPa). The simulation protocol involved individually substituting these core materials into the stator and rotor domains while holding all other parameters constant—specifically, the excitation source (Ceramic 8D magnets) and the conductor phase (Copper-75 C). This ceteris paribus approach isolates the core material’s influence on the machine’s macroscopic performance. The resulting performance matrix, detailed in Table  6 , quantifies the variations in Output Power, Electromagnetic Torque, System Efficiency, and Net Mass.

The quantitative results presented in Table  6  reveal distinct performance hierarchies governed by the density and loss characteristics of each alloy. The Nanocrystalline (Finemet FT-3 M) and Amorphous (Metglas 2605HB1M) grades emerged as the superior candidates for lightweight, high-efficiency applications. Both materials achieved the highest system efficiency of 67.88% and 67.87% respectively, while simultaneously recording the lowest net weights (~ 2.36 kg). This correlation suggests that their advanced microstructures effectively minimize core hysteresis, translating directly to reduced total losses (~ 1.183 kW).

In contrast, the Nickel-Iron (Permalloy 2mil) variant matched the peak efficiency of Finemet (67.88%) but incurred a significant gravimetric penalty, resulting in the highest net weight of 2.71 kg. This confirms that while NiFe alloys offer exceptional permeability, their high mass density makes them less suitable for weight-critical traction motors compared to amorphous alternatives.

The Soft Magnetic Composite (Somaloy 700 h) exhibited the lowest performance metrics in this specific topology, recording the highest total loss (1.22 kW) and the lowest efficiency (67.19%). While SMCs offer isotropic flux advantages for 3D geometries, their lower magnetic permeability and higher hysteresis losses compared to laminated steels render them less efficient in standard axial flux configurations where 2D flux flow predominates. Consequently, for this specific 2.5 kW motor design, Nanocrystalline and Amorphous cores represent the superior design choice, offering a ~ 12.8% weight reduction compared to Permalloy with no penalty in electrical efficiency.

The simulation data reveals a counter-intuitive plateau: despite significant variations in specific core loss (ranging from 1.18 kW to 1.22 kW) and net rotor/stator weight, the overall system efficiency remains restricted to a remarkably narrow bandwidth (67.19%–67.88%). This insensitivity is a direct consequence of the magnetic loading regime. As validated by recent literature [ 156 ,  157 ] when high-permeability cores are paired with low-energy magnets (such as Ceramic 8D), the motor operates in a domain where efficiency is primarily dictated by Copper (I 2 R) and Magnet losses. Essentially, the low flux density of the ferrite magnet fails to drive the core materials near their saturation limits, rendering variations in specific iron loss negligible in the broader power balance. This dynamic is fundamentally inverted when the excitation source is upgraded to a high-energy density material. As evidenced by the data for NdFeB-35 (summarized in Table  7 ), introducing a strong rare-earth magnet exposes the true performance variance between core alloys. Under this high-flux condition, the superior saturation and permeability of Cobalt-Iron become critical differentiators; specifically, the Vacoflux 50 variant achieves a peak efficiency of 90.29%, confirming that premium core materials yield substantial efficiency gains only when paired with commensurate high-performance magnetic sources.

As detailed in Table  7 , the introduction of high-energy NdFeB-35 magnets radically alters the performance landscape. Unlike the ferrite-based baseline, which compressed all materials into a narrow efficiency band, the high-flux regime exposes a broad divergence in material capabilities, as illustrated in Fig.  20 . The system efficiency spans a significant range of 80.78% using M19 steel to a peak of 90.29% using vacoflux50 accompanied by a twofold variation in total losses (0.269 kW to 0.595 kW). This heightened sensitivity is driven by the physics of magnetic loading. The superior energy product ((BH) max ) of the NdFeB magnets pushes the operational flux density (B) much higher into the saturation region of the core. Under these elevated conditions, iron-core losses transition from a secondary factor to a dominant contributor in the total loss budget. Consequently, the distinct advantages of low-loss materials (such as Vacoflux or Amorphous alloys) are fully realized, amplifying their impact on overall machine efficiency. However, as outlined in Table  8 , these electromagnetic gains must be contextualized alongside the corresponding active material mass and estimated financial costs. The data reveals a stark financial contrast, achieving peak efficiency with Vacoflux50 incurs an estimated total cost of ₹26,038.86/kg, which is over thirteen times the cost of standard M19 steel (₹1,932.62/kg). Meanwhile, amorphous options like Metglas-2605HB1M provide a highly effective compromise, yielding the lowest net system weight (2.50 kg) at a fraction of the premium cost (₹3,438.32/kg). The resulting performance-cost trade-off shown in Fig.  21  illustrates this non-linear relationship, where the marginal financial cost of efficiency increases exponentially at the upper limits. This confirms a critical design corollary: in rare-earth permanent magnet machines, the selection of the core material is not merely a weight reduction exercise, but a decisive factor in defining the fundamental efficiency limit of the powertrain [ 156 ,  158 ]. sections.heading: Influence of permanent magnet materials in AF-PMSM
paragraphs: Following the core material analysis, the second phase of the study investigates the impact of the magnetic excitation source. For this sensitivity sweep, the stator core was fixed to Vacoflux 50 (0.35 mm)—the highest-performing alloy identified in Sect.  6.1 —to ensure the magnetic circuit could support high flux densities without premature saturation. The winding material remained constant as Copper-75 C. Two premium rare-earth magnet grades were evaluated against the baseline: (1) Samarium-Cobalt (SmCo28): Representing high-temperature stability and (2) Neodymium-Iron-Boron (N52): Representing maximum energy density.

The performance metrics for these configurations are detailed in Table  11 . As further illustrated by the efficiency comparison in Fig.  22 , the data indicates a decisive hierarchy in efficiency driven by the Maximum Energy Product ((BH) max ) of the materials. The advanced NdFeB grade (N52) achieved the pinnacle of performance, recording a system efficiency of 92.07% with a minimal total loss of 0.21545 kW, compared to the 87.66% efficiency and 0.35189 kW loss seen in the SmCo28 variant This superior output is directly attributable to the material’s extreme energy product (typically 380–420 kJ/m³ [ 63 ]), which generates a stronger air-gap flux density and consequently higher electromagnetic torque for the same input current. In contrast, the SmCo28 variant falls short of the N52 benchmark due to the lower intrinsic energy product of Samarium-Cobalt typically 160–220 kJ/m³.

Beyond pure electromagnetic capabilities, the physical mass and financial implications of utilizing these permanent magnets are outlined in Table  9 . The data reveals that the N52 configuration is not only more efficient but also approximately 1.5% lighter (2.6997 kg) and more cost-effective (₹23,017.63/kg) than the heavier (2.74268 kg) and more expensive SmCo28 (₹24,687.69/kg) alternative.
