While SmCo magnets offer indispensable advantages in terms of thermal stability and corrosion resistance, this study confirms that for applications where peak efficiency is the primary figure of merit (and operating temperatures are within standard limits), N52 NdFeB remains the superior choice. Its elevated coercivity ensures resistance to demagnetization under load, while its superior flux generation capability maximizes the power density of the AF-PMSM topology.

sections.heading: Influence of conductor materials in AF-PMSM
paragraphs: The final phase of the refinement process focuses on the stator windings, the primary source of resistive losses. For this investigation, the motor topology was locked to the high-performance configuration identified in the previous steps: a Vacoflux 50 core (for saturation handling) paired with N52 NdFeB magnets (for maximum flux density).
Fig. 24 Efficiency comparison of conductor materials
Fig. 25 Performance-cost trade-off analysis comparing electromagnetic efficiency and estimated active material cost for candidate conductor materials

The comparative performance metrics for the tested conductors—ranging from traditional metals to advanced nanocomposites—are summarized in Table  12 . As further illustrated by the efficiency comparison in Fig.  24 , the data establishes Carbon Nanotube-Copper (CNT-Cu) composites as the definitive performance leader. The CNT-Cu configuration achieved a peak system efficiency of 93.61%, with total losses suppressed to 0.01707 kW. Remarkably, as detailed in the active material mass breakdown in Table  10 , this material also contributed to the lowest system weight (2.41 kg), matching the pure CNT variant. This represents a significant 10.7% reduction in net motor weight compared to the standard Copper_75C configuration (2.70 kg) This indicates that CNT-Cu successfully bridges the gap, offering the conductivity of metal with the lightweight properties of carbon. Among pure metals, Silver (Ag) demonstrated the highest efficiency (95.95%), marginally outperforming the industry-standard Copper (95.75%). However, both metals incur a weight penalty (~ 2.7–2.76 kg) compared to the nanocomposites. Furthermore, Table  10  highlights the critical economic trade-off, while pure Silver achieves the efficiency pinnacle, its estimated active material cost (₹60,048.57/kg) is double that of the CNT-Cu composite (₹30,750.25/kg). The Aluminum (Al) and CNT-Al variants, while lightweight (2.46 kg), exhibited the lowest efficiencies (both at 91.22%). The higher resistivity of the aluminum matrix resulted in elevated armature copper losses (0.097 kW), confirming that for high-performance density, aluminum remains a compromise solution. Ultimately, synthesizing these physical requirements with their financial implications yields the comprehensive performance-cost trade-off analysis depicted in Fig.  25 . This visualization confirms that the CNT-Cu composite occupies the most favorable position on the Pareto front, offering an optimal balance of high efficiency, minimized weight, and competitive cost compared to both raditional and precious metal conductors for the AF-PMSM topology.

To visualize the magnitude of these improvements, Fig.  26  superimposes the efficiency map of the Final Proposed Design (Vacoflux 50 + N52 + CNT-Cu) against the original Base Motor (M19 + Ceramic + Copper).
Fig. 26 Efficiency comparison of base motor and final design

The contrast represents a paradigm shift in machine performance. While the Base Motor (green trace) peaks at a modest 67–68% efficiency, the Final Design (red trace) maintains a broad efficiency plateau approaching 94%. Quantitatively, the proposed architecture represents an absolute efficiency gain of approximately 26%. More critically, the total losses have been slashed from the baseline’s ~ 1.2 kW to just 0.171 kW—a staggering 85.71% reduction. This result confirms that the holistic integration of advanced soft magnetic alloys, high-energy rare-earth magnets, and nanocomposite conductors is not merely an incremental step, but a transformative strategy for next-generation electric propulsion.

sections.heading: Inferences
paragraphs: The comprehensive parametric analysis yields a fundamental design insight: the impact of material selection is not isolated but strictly coupled to the machine’s magnetic loading regime. In architectures utilizing low-energy excitation (Ceramic 8D), the system efficiency is effectively clamped within a narrow bandwidth (67.19%–67.88%). Despite measurable variations in specific iron losses (1.18–1.22 kW) and mass (2.36–2.71 kg), the overwhelming dominance of ohmic and magnet losses renders the choice of core material secondary. This confirms that in ferrite-based designs, the electromagnetic “bottleneck” is the low air-gap flux density, which prevents premium core alloys from providing a meaningful return on investment.

The integration of high-energy NdFeB magnets fundamentally alters this dynamic. The elevated flux density amplifies the core’s hysteresis and eddy current behaviors, resulting in a massive efficiency divergence of 80.78%–90.29%. Under these demanding conditions, Vacoflux 50 (0.35 mm) emerges as the requisite enabler, achieving superior efficiency (90.29%) by effectively managing the saturation limits that handicap lesser steels.

The study culminates in a definitive “Best-in-Class” topology. By synergizing the high saturation of Vacoflux 50, the energy density of N52 magnets, and the hyper-conductivity of CNT-Cu composites, the motor achieves a peak efficiency of 93.61%. This configuration suppresses total losses to just 0.1707 kW—representing a 85.71% reduction relative to the baseline motor. Critically, this transition is not merely an efficiency gain but a simultaneous improvement in power density; the CNT-Cu variant achieves a 10.7% reduction in net active material mass (2.41 kg) compared to the standard copper configuration (2.70 kg).

The results establish a clear hierarchy for conductor selection in high-performance traction: CNT-Cu > Pure CNT > Silver > Copper > Aluminum. While Aluminum offers weight advantages, its resistive penalty precludes it from ultra-high-efficiency tiers. Consequently, the data confirms that realizing the full potential of the AF-PMSM requires a holistic strategy: pairing advanced soft magnetic alloys with rare-earth magnets to drive flux, and utilizing nanocomposites to minimize the resulting thermal penalty.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This review has systematically evaluated the intersection of advanced material science and Axial Flux Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motor (AF-PMSM) design, revealing that the path to next-generation electric propulsion lies not in isolated component upgrades, but in holistic system integration. The comprehensive analysis of magnetic and conductive materials establishes three critical paradigms:

The Hierarchy of Magnetic Cores: While Silicon Steel remains the economic baseline, the study confirms that Cobalt-Iron (CoFe) alloys are indispensable for high-power-density applications due to their superior saturation limits. Conversely, for high-frequency architectures where minimizing core loss is paramount, Nanocrystalline and Amorphous alloys offer the highest efficiency ceilings. The emergence of Soft Magnetic Composites (SMC) represents a geometric breakthrough, enabling isotropic 3D flux paths that allow for complex, modular stator topologies previously impossible with laminated steels. The Imperative of High-Energy Excitation: The parametric case study empirically validated that the choice of core material is strictly coupled to the magnetic source. Under low-flux ferrite excitation, system efficiency is stagnant (~ 67%); however, the integration of high-energy NdFeB magnets acts as a force multiplier, exposing the true capabilities of advanced cores and elevating efficiency to the ~ 90% tier. While Samarium-Cobalt (SmCo) offers essential thermal stability for harsh environments, NdFeB remains the definitive standard for maximizing torque density in traction applications. The Conductor Revolution: The investigation into stator windings identified Carbon Nanotube (CNT) composites as the frontier of performance. By surpassing the conductivity-to-weight ratio of copper and silver, CNT-Cu composites enabled the modeled system to achieve a peak efficiency of 93.61%, slashing total losses by over 94% compared to the baseline design. This underscores that overcoming the “copper limit” is the final hurdle in minimizing thermal overhead.

Final Verdict: The transition from a baseline efficiency of ~ 67% to a peak of ~ 94% demonstrates that material selection is the single most deterministic factor in AF-PMSM performance. Future industrial success will depend on bridging the “lab-to-fab” gap—specifically, scaling the manufacturing of nanocomposites and developing sustainable, dysprosium-free magnet supply chains. Ultimately, the synergy of high-saturation cores, rare-earth permanent magnets, and nanocomposite conductors constitutes the definitive roadmap for achieving the aggressive power density targets required by the future of electric mobility.
